readerTitle: Why your own cash is never free money
caseNote: 가상 사례 (도장 회사, IT 지원 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 돈의 비용은 이자 고지서가 아니라 그 돈이 다른 곳에서 벌 수 있었던 수익으로 정해진다. 투자는 그 비용보다 더 벌 때만 의미가 있다.
misconception: 이자를 내지 않는 내 돈이나 상환 의무가 없는 투자금은 공짜이니, 조금이라도 수익이 나면 쓰는 게 이득이다.

sources.text: 기업재무의 표준 개념 (자본비용, 기회비용, 위험과 요구수익률)

factChecks.note: softwareNote의 벤처 투자자 기대 수익은 구체적 수치 없이 일반적으로만 서술했습니다. 수치를 추가하려면 출처를 먼저 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why your own cash is never free money
body: A painting company has $60,000 sitting in the bank from good years. The owner wants a new spray rig. "It's our own money," she says. "No interest, no bank. Any return is a win."
It sounds like the safest kind of spending. It can quietly be one of the most expensive.

image.label: Stack of cash with a hidden price tag
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작업복을 입은 도장 회사 사장이 현금 더미를 페인트 분무 장비 쪽으로 밀고 있음. 현금 더미 뒤에 반쯤 숨겨진 가격표가 달려 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: Should she buy the rig with her cash?
body: The rig costs $60,000 and should add about $3,000 of profit a year. That's a 5% return.
The company also still owes $60,000 on an older equipment loan at 10% interest. Savings in the bank earn about 2%.

options.text: Yes. It's idle cash, so any profit beats zero
options.feedback: The cash isn't really idle. Treating it as free hides better uses, so a weak project looks like a win.

options.text: Yes. 5% beats the 2% the bank pays
options.feedback: Good instinct to compare. But the bank isn't the best alternative here, and the comparison stops too early.

options.text: First compare it with paying off the 10% loan
options.feedback: Right. Paying down the loan "earns" 10% with almost no risk. The rig has to beat that, and it doesn't.

cards.title: Same $60,000, three uses.
body: The rig earns $3,000. Paying off the loan saves $6,000. Choosing the rig leaves **$3,000 a year** on the table, even though no bank charged a cent.

cards.title: The cost of capital
body: **The cost of capital** is the return money must earn to be worth using. It's set by what the people supplying it could get elsewhere for a similar risk.
For a loan, that's the interest rate. For your own cash, it's what the money gives up: the next-best use. Here that was 10%, not zero.
A project creates value only when it earns more than the cost of the money behind it.

image.label: Project return bar compared with a cost-of-money line
image.brief: 막대 그래프. "Project return 5%" 막대가 "Cost of the money 10%"라는 가로 점선 아래에 있음. 점선 위는 초록 "Creates value", 아래는 빨강 "Destroys value" 영역으로 표시.

cards.title: Every source of money has a price.
body: The price rises with the risk the provider takes.
list: **Bank loan:** the interest rate. Often the cheapest, because lenders get paid first.
**Your own cash:** what it could earn elsewhere, plus the risk you carry as owner.
**Outside investors:** usually the highest, because they get paid last and take the most risk.
cards.callout: The money with no monthly bill is often the most expensive.
cards.softwareNote: Software founders often feel venture money is free because there are no repayments. But investors expect returns far above any loan rate. Spending it on a growth channel that barely pays back loses value, even if the bank balance looks healthy.

cards.title: One project, two verdicts.
body: Picture a $100,000 project that earns 12% a year, or $12,000.
Fund it with an 8% loan and you pay $8,000 in interest. You're **$4,000 ahead**.
Fund it with investors who expect 20% and they're owed $20,000 of value. You're $8,000 behind.
The project didn't change. The cost of the money did. That's why "is this a good project?" has no answer until you know what's paying for it.

cards.title: It's an estimate, and cheap money has its own costs.
body: For a small business, the cost of capital is a rough range, not a precise figure. Use it to catch clearly bad deals, not to split hairs over half a percent.

Also, the cheapest money isn't automatically the best. A loan adds fixed payments that hurt in a slow month. And keeping some cash as a **safety cushion** is a real use too. Protection against a bad season counts as a return.

cards.title: Now it's an IT support firm.
body: You fix computers and networks for local offices. Hiring and training two technicians for a new service line costs $80,000 and should add about $8,000 a year: 10%.
The bank offers a loan at 9%. A friend offers $80,000 for a share of profits and hopes to earn about 25% a year. What do you do?

options.text: Take the friend's money. No repayments means no cost
options.feedback: No payments, but a 25% expectation. The project earns $8,000 against $20,000 your friend hopes for. That gap lands on you or the friendship.

options.text: Take the bank loan. 10% still beats 9%
options.feedback: It does, by only $800 a year. A small miss in your estimate turns it into a loss, and you'd carry fixed payments too.

options.text: Rework the plan until it clearly beats the cost of the money
options.feedback: You give up speed but avoid a project that barely covers its funding. Try a smaller start, one hire, or a higher price for the service.

cards.title: Money is never free. Know its price before you spend it.
body: A project is worth funding only if it earns more than the money behind it costs, including your own cash.

**Try it today:** take your next planned purchase. Write its expected yearly return as a percent. Next to it, write the cost of the money you'd use: the loan rate, or the best other thing that cash could do.
